meta: Ask one AI to research 20 competitors, and by number 10 it starts forgetting number 1. Because each AI has a limited "desk", called the context window. Multi-agent splits the job among several AIs.

muc.title: One AI, twenty competitors
muc.text: Give one AI a big job: research twenty competitors, reading a dozen web pages for each. By competitor number ten, it starts forgetting competitor number one.

muc.title: The desk has a limit
muc.text: Because each AI has a limited desk, called the context window, as video 9 explained. Pile on too many documents, and the desk overflows.

muc.title: Orchestrator and subagents
muc.text: The fix: split the work among many agents, called multi-agent. A lead agent, called the orchestrator, makes a plan and gives each subagent a few competitors. Each subagent has its own context window, they run at the same time, and when they're done they only send back a short summary.

muc.title: Anthropic tried it
muc.text: Anthropic tried this for Claude's research feature. An orchestrator with several subagents did up to ninety percent better than a single agent, on their internal test.

muc.title: A big team is expensive
muc.text: But a big team is expensive: in total it uses about fifteen times the tokens of a normal chat. So it's only worth it for big jobs that can be split into independent parts.

muc.title: You be the lead AI
muc.text: For a big job like planning a trip to three cities, open three chats, one for each place. Then paste the three summaries into a fourth chat to put it all together. You just acted as the orchestrator.

muc.title: Who's in charge?
muc.text: Now there's a team. Who's in charge, and who checks the work? Part six.
